podcast.title: Car Accident Leading to MRI Confirmation
podcast.body: In April 2017, Art Alexakis was involved in a car accident when his vehicle's brakes failed while driving to pick up his daughter, resulting in a collision with a Jeep. Though everyone involved was unharmed, a subsequent "twinge in his arm" two weeks later prompted an MRI scan, which ultimately revealed the MS lacerations on his brain, confirming his diagnosis. "That was how he discovered he had MS lacerations on his brain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Concealment and Public Perception
podcast.body: Initially, Alexakis kept his MS diagnosis private. However, as symptoms like stumbling and forgetting lyrics emerged on stage, observers began to speculate whether he was struggling with alcohol or drug use, unaware of his underlying health condition. "He kept a quiet for a long time, but then he started stumbling a bit and forgetting lyrics on stage, and people began to wonder if he was drinking or on drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis
podcast.body: In 2017, Art Alexakis, the leader of Everclear, was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS), a disease that targets the central nervous system by attacking the protective coating around nerve fibers. This condition can lead to a range of issues, including problems with walking, vision, and chronic fatigue. "In 2017, he was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, a disease of the central nervous system."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Positive Prognosis and Treatment
podcast.body: Despite the diagnosis, Art Alexakis maintains a generally good prognosis, with his MS condition currently under control. He manages the disease with three weekly injections of a drug called Copaxone, and while he experiences occasional vision issues, he is expected to live a full life. "The good news is that his prognosis is generally good. His condition is under control, thanks to three weekly injections of a drug called Cops Zone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: MS Diagnosis (April 2017)
xref.body: Art Alexakis began noticing symptoms in 2015, including stumbling and forgetting lyrics, which some mistook for drinking or drug use. He dismissed it as tiredness. After a car crash in April 2017 and a subsequent arm twinge, an MRI, arranged by his daughter, revealed lacerations on his brain indicative of multiple sclerosis. He kept the diagnosis quiet for four years. "Then in April 2017, he was on his way to pick up his daughter at school. It was raining, and he crashed into a jeep. Now nobody was hurt, but then two weeks later, he had a twinge in his arm that he thought was left over from a snowboarding crash or maybe the jeep crash. His daughter set him up with an MRI, and that's when he learned the news. They found lacerations on Art's brain indicative of multiple sclerosis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: Art Alexakis received "rave reviews" in a couple of categories on Donna's Domain, a website that rates rock stars' penis size and sexual ability. xref.title: Managing Multiple Sclerosis
xref.body: Initially viewing his MS diagnosis as a death sentence, Art Alexakis's prognosis improved after working with doctors who prescribed Copazone. He takes three injections a week, avoids inflammatory foods like sugar, and has been told by his doctor he could have another 30 years if his condition remains stable. While he can no longer run and has taken up swimming, his guitar playing remains unaffected, and he doesn't expect to be confined to a wheelchair. "The prognosis isn't as bad as he thought it might be, and Art realizes that he may need a cane later in life, but he shouldn't be confined to a wheelchair. He hopes. He gives himself three injections a week, yes to stay away from inflammatory foods like sugar, and if things continue the way they are, Art's doctor says he could have another 30 years."
